analysis.investment_thesis: Park Medi World is a regional NCR hospital chain riding India's genuine healthcare tailwind, but it's priced at 44x earnings while delivering only 3.3% net profit CAGR over four years — a PEG ratio north of 13, which is indefensible. Rising finance costs (26.3% CAGR) are quietly suffocating bottom-line growth even as revenue expands at 16%.
key_strengths: Solid ROE/ROCE of 21%/20% with NABH-accredited multi-specialty hospitals — genuine quality franchise in NCR
Revenue growing 16.1% CAGR driven by real secular tailwind of Indian healthcare underpenetration
Consistently positive OCF (5/5 years) and D/E of 0.58 — just within Lynch's 0.6 threshold
key_risks: Earnings growth catastrophically lags revenue: net profit CAGR is only 3.3% vs 16.1% revenue — the story is not translating to shareholders
Finance costs ballooned from ₹24 Cr to ₹61 Cr (+155% over 4Y), and borrowings jumped from ₹292 Cr to ₹734 Cr — debt is eating the business alive
Valuation is grotesque for the growth delivered: P/E 44x on 3.3% earnings growth = PEG ~13x; even using revenue growth gives PEG of 2.75x — Lynch threshold is 1.0x
red_flags: Net profit collapsed 33% in FY2024 (₹228 Cr → ₹152 Cr) — highly volatile earnings for a supposedly defensive hospital business
Promoter holds 82.89% — institutional interest minimal (FII only 0.86%), limiting re-rating catalyst
FCF swung from ₹294 Cr (2024) to just ₹66 Cr (2025) as capex surged to ₹159 Cr — capital intensity rising without commensurate earnings lift
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Park Medi World has a coherent story — a branded multi-specialty hospital network in one of India's wealthiest urban markets, serving real and growing demand. The ROE of 21% and consistent OCF positivity suggest the underlying business model works. But as a Lynch investor, I want earnings growth, and this company is giving me 3.3% net profit CAGR at a P/E of 44. That's a PEG ratio of roughly 13 — I won't touch anything above 1.5, let alone 13. The culprit is clear: finance costs compounding at 26.3% annually are consuming the operating leverage that revenue growth should be delivering.

The FY2024 earnings crash (down 33% year-on-year to ₹152 Cr) is a serious warning sign for a "defensive" healthcare business. FY2025 recovery to ₹213 Cr barely matches FY2023 levels, meaning zero net progress in two years. Meanwhile, the company has been aggressively adding fixed assets (CWIP jumped to ₹54 Cr, capex hit ₹159 Cr in FY2025) — a bet on future capacity that hasn't yet produced earnings. Until debt costs stabilize, margins expand meaningfully, and EPS grows consistently above 15%, this stock at ₹216 and ₹9,350 Cr market cap is a story with a great backdrop but a broken financial narrative. Pass.
